common_name: Sessantina Grossa Broccoli Raab (Large Italian 60-Day Rapini)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; broccoli raab bolts quickly once days lengthen and warm, so time plantings for cool weather.

directions: Sessantina Grossa is a classic Italian landrace broccoli raab whose name translates roughly to 'big sixty-day,' describing its larger leaves and buds compared to faster, smaller rapini types. Direct sow thickly in cool weather and thin as needed, harvesting whole young plants or cutting the central shoot with its small flower buds once they appear but before petals open. The deeply lobed, dark green leaves and slightly nutty, pleasantly bitter buds are traditionally sauteed with garlic and olive oil or added to soups and pasta dishes. Keep soil consistently moist and harvest promptly, since heat brings on rapid bolting and increased bitterness.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Direct sow from early spring through late summer for successive cool-season harvests; this hybrid holds quality a bit longer into warm weather than older open-pollinated raab types.

directions: Zamboni is a modern hybrid broccoli raab bred for a longer harvest window and better bolt tolerance than traditional Italian landrace rapini. Direct sow in rows and begin cutting the tender central shoots with their small unopened flower buds about six to seven weeks after sowing, which encourages side-shoot production for repeat harvests. Leaves, stems, and buds are all edible with the same assertive, mustardy-bitter flavor typical of broccoli raab, best tamed by a quick saute with garlic and chili flakes. Because it tolerates a slightly wider temperature range than older varieties, it is a useful choice for extending the rapini harvest into early summer or starting it earlier in fall.

planting.note: Direct sow in earliest workable spring soil; this variety was selected specifically for spring planting without the premature bolting that affects many raab types sown before long days arrive.

directions: Spring Raab was bred by Oregon plant breeder Frank Morton specifically to solve broccoli raab's biggest flaw: most varieties were selected for fall planting and bolt to seed almost immediately if sown in spring's lengthening days. This selection holds its vegetative, leafy-budded stage longer under spring conditions, giving a reliable harvest window instead of an instant bolt. Cut the central flowering shoot once small buds form but before yellow petals show, then continue picking side shoots for several weeks. Flavor is milder and less bitter than many older raab landraces, making it a good entry point for gardeners new to the crop.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost for an early crop, or direct sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop that often sizes up sweeter in cool weather.

directions: Korist is a widely grown commercial F1 kohlrabi producing uniform, pale green globes with crisp, mild white flesh that resists getting woody as bulbs size up. Its even bolt resistance and uniform maturity make it a dependable choice for successive plantings through spring and fall. Harvest when bulbs reach tennis-ball size for the best balance of tenderness and flavor, peeling the outer skin before eating raw in slaws or cooked in soups and stir-fries. Keep soil evenly moist, since drought stress toughens the bulb and can trigger premature bolting.

common_name: Azur Star Kohlrabi (F1 Hybrid Purple Kohlrabi)

planting.note: Start indoors ahead of the last frost for a spring harvest, or direct sow in late summer; purple skin color develops best with cool nights.

directions: Azur Star is a commercial F1 purple kohlrabi valued for its deep violet skin, uniform round shape, and white flesh that stays crisp and mild rather than fibrous at harvest size. The uniform habit and consistent bulb shape make it well suited to both home gardens and market growers wanting an attractive bunching crop. Harvest at 2-3 inches in diameter for the sweetest, most tender eating, slicing raw for salads and vegetable trays or cooking briefly to retain its crunch. Provide steady moisture and full sun, and succession sow every few weeks for a continuous supply through the cool season.

common_name: Eder Kohlrabi (Early F1 Hybrid Green Kohlrabi)

planting.note: Start indoors early for the first harvest of the season; Eder's speed to maturity makes it a good choice for gardeners wanting kohlrabi before the main spring crop comes in.

directions: Eder is a fast-maturing green kohlrabi hybrid bred for an especially short time to harvest, reaching usable bulb size well ahead of standard varieties. Its compact habit and quick turnaround suit tight succession plantings or gardeners looking to slot a crop into a short cool-weather window. Pick bulbs promptly once they reach 2-3 inches across, since early types can turn woody faster than slower-maturing kohlrabi if left in the ground too long. Flesh is crisp and mild, equally good sliced raw or added to stir-fries and soups.

planting.note: Propagate from stem cuttings rooted in spring once frost danger passes; Purple Tree Collard rarely sets viable seed and is grown almost entirely from vegetative cuttings of an existing plant.

directions: Purple Tree Collard is a perennial, non-flowering collard selection that grows a tall, woody, cane-like stalk topped with a rosette of broad, purple-tinged blue-green leaves, living for years in frost-free or mild-winter climates rather than completing its life cycle in one season. Root sturdy stem cuttings in moist potting mix or water, then set out in rich, well-drained soil in full sun, staking tall canes as they grow top-heavy. Harvest lower leaves continuously as the plant grows taller, leaving the top rosette intact, which encourages a steady supply of tender, mildly sweet, slightly purple-tinted greens that many gardeners find milder than annual collards. In climates with hard freezes it can be grown as a large annual or overwintered indoors as a potted cutting, since it typically does not survive temperatures much below the mid-20s Fahrenheit.
sources: UC Santa Cruz Center for Agroecology

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; chinense types germinate slowly and erratically without steady warmth.

directions: Jamaican Yellow Scotch Bonnet produces the classic squat, bonnet-shaped pods of the type, ripening to bright yellow with the fruity, almost tropical aroma that distinguishes true scotch bonnets from habaneros of similar heat. Heat runs in roughly the same 100,000-350,000 Scoville range as habanero but with a sweeter, less sharply acidic flavor that is prized in Jamaican jerk seasoning and Caribbean hot sauces. Give plants a long, warm season, steady moisture, and full sun, and expect a heavy main flush of fruit in late summer. Handle ripe pods with gloves and harvest once fully colored for the best balance of heat and characteristic fruity flavor.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this variety is slow and erratic to germinate even by chinense standards.

directions: 7 Pot Red is the original Trinidadian 7 Pot pepper from which the many modern 7 Pot strains (Douglah, Primo, Barrackpore, Bubblegum, and others) were later selected, named for the Trinidad claim that a single pod could flavor seven pots of stew. Pods are wrinkled, roughly bell-shaped with a small tail, ripening from green to a deep glossy red, with heat commonly falling in the 800,000-1,000,000 Scoville range alongside a sweet, fruity flavor. Give plants a long, warm growing season and full sun, since pods can take well over 100 days from transplant to fully ripen and develop their characteristic wrinkled skin. Handle ripe fruit with gloves and avoid touching eyes or skin, as oils linger on hands long after harvest.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Bonda Ma Jacques Pepper (French Antillean Habanero-Type Chile)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; chinense types need sustained warmth to germinate reliably.

directions: Bonda Ma Jacques is a traditional habanero-type chile from the French Caribbean islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique, producing elongated, slightly wrinkled pods that ripen from green to yellow-orange with the characteristic fruity, floral chinense aroma. Heat is milder than most scotch bonnets or habaneros, generally in the low-to-mid habanero range, making it useful where chinense flavor is wanted without extreme heat. Give plants full sun, a long warm season, and consistent moisture, since pods develop slowly and ripen over an extended harvest window. It is used throughout the French Antilles in sauces, marinades, and the spicy condiment known locally as sauce chien.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or start in midsummer for transplanting out for a fall crop, which often produces the most reliable, best-colored heads.

directions: Depurple is a hybrid purple cauliflower bred to hold its deep violet curd color evenly in full sun, unlike many older purple types that fade or develop uneven patches of green or white where leaves don't fully shade the head. No blanching or leaf-tying is needed, simplifying care compared to white cauliflower. The anthocyanin pigments responsible for the color hold up reasonably well through light cooking, so it keeps much of its visual appeal steamed or roasted, though prolonged boiling will still mute it. Grow with the same steady moisture, rich soil, and even temperatures that white cauliflower needs, since heat stress or dry spells can cause small, buttoned heads regardless of color.

planting.note: Direct sow from early spring through fall; Savannah tolerates more heat than many komatsuna types without bolting, extending the harvest window into warmer weather.

directions: Savannah is a komatsuna selection bred for improved heat and bolt tolerance compared to older Japanese mustard spinach varieties, letting it be sown over a longer part of the season. Leaves are smooth, glossy, and dark green on slender white stalks, with a mild flavor closer to spinach than to sharper mustard greens. Harvest whole young plants for salad mix or cut individual outer leaves from more mature plants, which regrow readily for repeat picking. It performs equally well raw in salads or lightly cooked in stir-fries and soups, wilting quickly like true spinach.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring for a summer crop, or in late summer for a fall and winter harvest; flavor sweetens noticeably after frost.

directions: Ragged Jack is an open-pollinated heirloom kale in the Red Russian family, with deeply serrated, oak-leaf-shaped gray-green leaves veined in purplish-red that deepens with cool fall temperatures. It is tender enough to eat raw in salads while young, becoming better suited to cooking as leaves mature and toughen slightly. Long grown and seed-saved in Southern gardens, it tolerates both summer heat and winter cold better than many curly kale types, often overwintering in milder zones to provide an extended harvest. Harvest outer leaves continuously from the base, leaving the growing crown intact for continued production over many months.
